caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:pag-1
attempts.entry_title: Threat probability in ventrolateral periaqueductal gray neurons (Wright and McDannald 2019)
attempts.summary: The paper's main findings held up in this data: ventrolateral periaqueductal gray neurons form Onset and Ramping populations of the reported sizes, both discriminate danger, uncertainty and safety, and single-trial regressions show their firing tracks threat probability over fear output. Several regression results hold only under the nose poke baselines and 0/0 rule that reproduce the paper's printed regression table on one neuron, which the paper does not state. The Figure 4 single-neuron correlations are no stronger than the Z-scoring produces. Seven claims held only in part, among them when danger and uncertainty firing diverge, the count of Onset-Ramping pairs and how many neurons' delay and post-shock betas correlate (3 of 20 against 13). No claim was blocked.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Wright and McDannald (2019) on CRCNS data set pag-1, which holds the spike times, event times and mean waveforms of 245 ventrolateral periaqueductal gray units recorded in 88 fear discrimination sessions of six rats. It recomputes suppression ratios, the k-means clusters, the Onset and Ramping populations, their population and single-unit firing, and the single-unit regressions on threat probability and fear output, under every reading of the details the paper leaves open and the reading the paper's printed regression input fixes.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Wright and McDannald (2019) from CRCNS pag-1

outcomes.statement: Over the 88 recording sessions, suppression ratio over the whole 10 s cue differs by cue, high to danger (0.80), intermediate to uncertainty (0.53) and low to safety (0.03), and each cue pair differs.
outcomes.source: Results, first section, paragraph 2 (after Figure 1 supplements); Figure 1C
outcomes.quote: Across all 88 recording sessions, these six rats showed excellent discriminative fear ... high to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and low to safety

statistics.about: cue effect, one-way ANOVA over danger, uncertainty and safety

outcomes.notes: Over 88 sessions all eight readings of the amended claims file (total fear over 10 s or 20 s, each 0/0 rule, both session values) put the three means within tolerance, and their tests hold. Under the first reading the criterion lists (10 s, 0/0 set to 0, mean of the per-trial ratios), given as measured, danger is 0.768, uncertainty 0.502 and safety -0.002. With the 20 s baseline and 0/0 set to 1, the reading the Methods regression table fixes, they are 0.799, 0.531 and 0.030; the repeated-measures ANOVA of cue gives F(2,174) = 595, p = 1.6e-78, danger against uncertainty t(87) = 12.3, p = 9.1e-21, and uncertainty against safety t = 21.0, p = 7.8e-36 (paper F = 592.00, t = 12.36, t = 20.85). Danger is within tolerance of the legend's 0.83 under every reading (0.768 to 0.799). By rat, danger ranges from 0.29 (rf08, 3 sessions) to 0.94 (rf03). The answer to this attempt's question (questions/wright-2019.yaml) amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: total fear now has its own window, 10 s or 20 s, and 0/0 may be 1. The 2 s total fear readings, which put danger at 0.35 to 0.75, are no longer readings, so the outcome no longer depends on the window. The earlier run gave the measured values under the 20 s reading, as a deviation outside the claims file's readings; they are now under the first reading listed, and the deviation is withdrawn.

outcomes.statement: Suppression scales non-linearly with shock probability. Uncertainty's shock probability is closer to safety, but its mean suppression ratio is closer to danger.
outcomes.source: Results, first section, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: While the foot shock probability associated with uncertainty was closer to safety ... the mean suppression ratio to uncertainty was closer to danger
outcomes.notes: fig1c-total-suppression matched under all eight readings of the amended claims file, and under each the uncertainty mean is above the midpoint of the danger and safety means (first reading 0.502 against 0.383; 20 s with 0/0 set to 1, 0.531 against 0.415). The answer to this attempt's question (questions/wright-2019.yaml) amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: the readings on which fig1c-total-suppression matched are now all eight, where they were the 10 s and 20 s ones. The outcome is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: Suppression ratios in each 1 s cue interval discriminate every cue pair in every interval, with a cue effect and a cue x interval interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, first section, paragraph 3; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: When the total cue period was divided into 10, 1 s intervals, discrimination was observed in each interval and its pattern showed subtle change over cue presentation

statistics.about: cue effect, cue x interval ANOVA

outcomes.notes: With interval fear over the 2 s baseline (readings a and b of detail 1), 0/0 set to 1 (reading c of detail 2) and trial means, the cue effect is F(2,174) = 493 and the cue x interval interaction F(18,1566) = 6.15, p = 9.5e-15 (paper 489.40 and 6.21). Danger exceeds uncertainty and uncertainty exceeds safety at p < 0.005 in all ten intervals (smallest t 3.03 and 6.2; paper all t > 3.00 and > 7.00). Of the eight readings of the amended claims file (interval fear over 2 s or 10 s), the four with 0/0 set to 1 give 10 of 10 in both comparisons. The four with 0/0 set to 0 or left out give 8 or 9 of 10 danger-uncertainty intervals, which would be partially reproduced. All eight give 10 of 10 uncertainty-safety intervals and both ANOVA effects. The answer to this attempt's question (questions/wright-2019.yaml) amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: interval fear is now over 2 s or 10 s (20 s is no longer a reading for it), and 0/0 set to 1 is now reading c of detail 2. The outcome and the assumption stand, now on a reading the claims file lists; the readings that differ are those of the 0/0 rule, not of the window (earlier 5 of 12 readings gave 10 of 10, now 4 of 8).
deviations: The readings differ in outcome. The one adopted, 0/0 set to 1 (reading c of detail 2), is the rule of the Methods regression table, where trials with no poke in baseline or interval are 1.00, and of Figure 1, figure supplement 2 ("A suppression ratio of 1.0 is found ... when no poke occurs in an interval"). The question is for the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: Baseline nose poke rates do not differ between trial types, and poking falls from baseline to cue for danger and uncertainty but not for safety.
outcomes.source: Figure 1, figure supplement 1A
outcomes.quote: Baseline nose poke rates did not differ between trial types and rats showed significant reductions in poking to danger and uncertainty, but not safety

statistics.about: baseline against cue, per trial type

outcomes.notes: The amended claims file says the supplement uses the total fear window: 10 s under reading a of detail 1, 20 s under readings b and c. Under every window shown (2, 10 and 20 s), poking falls from baseline to cue for danger and both uncertainty types (t(87) from 10.6 to 17.6, all p < 1e-16) and not for safety (p 0.24 to 0.60). Baseline rates across the four trial types do not differ with the 10 s window (F(3,261) = 2.43, p = 0.066), where the claim is reproduced. They do differ with the 20 s window adopted here (F = 3.47, p = 0.017), where the means are 39.6, 37.0, 39.1 and 37.8 pokes/min. The former 2 s window gives F = 2.20, p = 0.088. The answer to this attempt's question (questions/wright-2019.yaml) amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: the baseline is now the total fear window, 10 s or 20 s. The 20 s window adopted earlier as an assumption outside the claims file's readings is now readings b and c, and the 2 s window is no longer a reading. The outcome and the assumption are unchanged.
deviations: The readings differ in outcome. The 20 s window (readings b and c of detail 1) is adopted as an assumption because it is the total fear baseline of the Methods regression table, and the one the data set's cubeScript.m stores as poke.base. The 10 s result is shown. The question is for the paper's authors (findings).

outcomes.statement: Suppression ratio and cue nose poke rate are significantly correlated across sessions, particularly for danger and uncertainty.
outcomes.source: Figure 1, figure supplement 1B
outcomes.quote: The two measures were significantly correlated, particularly for danger and uncertainty
outcomes.notes: Under every reading of the amended claims file the suppression ratio and the cue poke rate correlate negatively over the 88 sessions for danger (r -0.60 to -0.73) and uncertainty (r -0.67 to -0.75), all p < 1e-9, and over all 264 points (r -0.76 to -0.79). Safety correlates more weakly (r -0.30 to -0.35, p 0.001 to 0.005). The answer to this attempt's question (questions/wright-2019.yaml) amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: total fear is over 10 s or 20 s. The 2 s readings, now former, also gave negative danger and uncertainty correlations at p < 0.001; the outcome is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: K-means clustering (k = 2) of all 245 neurons on baseline firing rate, waveform half duration and amplitude ratio splits them on baseline firing rate alone into a low firing rate cluster of 199 and a high firing rate cluster of 46.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons are responsive at cue onset or ramp over cue presentation, paragraph 1; Methods, K-means clustering; Figure 1E
outcomes.quote: All neurons separated into one of two clusters purely on the basis of baseline firing rate ... with majority of neurons falling into the low firing rate (LFR) cluster (n = 199) and the remaining in the high firing rate (HFR) cluster (n = 46)

statistics.about: amplitude ratio and duration by cluster

outcomes.notes: With the mean rate in the 2 s before onset and raw features (reading a, a), k-means gives 197 LFR and 48 HFR neurons. The baseline rate differs by cluster (F(1,243) = 835, p = 1.4e-80; paper 829), and half duration (p = 0.97) and amplitude ratio (p = 0.51) do not. Z-scored features give 198 and 47 (also within tolerance). The session rate gives 194 and 51, with HFR outside tolerance. The files hold spikes only from 20 s before each onset to 31 to 34 s after it, so after verification round 1 the session rate is taken over the windows from 20 s before to 30 s after onset (the earlier run divided by the span of the train, about a third of the rate); the cluster sizes under that reading are unchanged.
deviations: The Methods define the waveform features in words. The peaks are picked as described in pag.py (largest deflection, the opposite extreme before and after it); the waveform has no unit. The k-means initialisation (k-means++ starts, 20 replicates, seed 0) is a standard choice.

outcomes.statement: 29 neurons (from 5 of 6 rats, about 12% of all) increase firing in the first 1 s of danger, uncertainty or safety over the 2 s pre-cue baseline, and all of them are in the LFR cluster. These are the Onset population.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons are responsive at cue onset or ramp over cue presentation, paragraph 2; Methods, Identifying cue-responsive vlPAG neurons
outcomes.quote: We identified 29 neurons (obtained from 5/6 rats, ~12% of all neurons recorded) with phasic increases in firing to danger, uncertainty, or safety ... All 29 neurons belonged to the LFR cluster
outcomes.notes: The Methods screen finds 29 Onset neurons from 5 rats (dr01 10, dr02 4, rf02 4, rf03 10, rf08 1), all in the LFR cluster under every clustering reading. Rounding the baseline rate down, as the data set's cubeScript.m does, would give 31 from 6 rats. One Onset neuron (dr02092716epr38aSPK04a) shares 66% of its spikes with another unit of its session (findings). The Onset neurons' half durations (0.038 to 0.200 ms) and amplitude ratios (0.13 to 1.00) are printed for comparison with Figure 1, figure supplement 4, which gives them only in a figure.

outcomes.statement: Of the remaining neurons, 17 increase firing over baseline in the last 1 s of at least one cue; three are in the HFR cluster, and the other 14 (from 4 of 6 rats, about 6%) are the Ramping population.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons are responsive at cue onset or ramp over cue presentation, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: 17 neurons increased firing to at least one cue during the last 1 s cue interval (interval > baseline, p<0.017). Three neurons belonged to the high firing cluster ... The remaining 14 neurons (obtained from 4/6 rats, ~6% of all neurons recorded) belonged to the LFR cluster
outcomes.notes: Of the other neurons, 17 pass the screen on the last 1 s. Three are in the HFR cluster under every clustering reading, and the 14 Ramping neurons come from 4 rats (dr01 4, dr02 2, rf02 1, rf03 7).

outcomes.statement: Onset population firing (100 ms bins, 1 s before to the end of the cue) shows main effects of cue and bin and a cue x bin interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 1; Figure 2A
outcomes.quote: revealed main effects of cue and bin (Fs > 9, ps<0.01, η p 2 > 0.20, op > 0.95) but most critically, a cue x bin interaction (F 218,6104 = 1.94, p<0.01

statistics.about: main effects of cue and bin

outcomes.statement: In the first 1 s cue interval Onset neurons fire more to danger than to uncertainty; firing to uncertainty is numerically but not significantly above safety, while an ANOVA over the first 5 s of uncertainty and safety shows a cue x bin interaction.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 1; Figure 2B, left
outcomes.quote: Onset neurons showed significantly greater firing to danger compared to uncertainty in the first 1 s cue interval (t 28 = 4.54, p=9.70×10 −5 ). While numerically greater firing to uncertainty over safety failed to reach significance in the first 1 s interval (t 28 = 1.37, p=0.18), ANOVA restricted to uncertainty and safety

statistics.about: uncertainty and safety, cue x bin, 1 s before onset to 5 s into the cue

outcomes.notes: Danger above uncertainty t(28) = 5.05, p = 2.4e-5 (paper 4.54, 9.70e-5). Uncertainty -0.09 against safety -0.23, t = 1.36, p = 0.185 (paper 1.37, 0.18). The uncertainty and safety ANOVA over 60 bins gives cue x bin F(59,1652) = 1.41, p = 0.024 (paper 1.50, 0.01). The type-baseline reading gives the same outcome. By rat, danger exceeds uncertainty in all five rats.

outcomes.statement: Differential firing of Onset neurons is absent in the last 1 s cue interval, for danger against uncertainty and uncertainty against safety.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 1; Figure 2B, right
outcomes.quote: Differential firing was not observed to danger vs. uncertainty (t 28 = 1.69, p=0.10) or to uncertainty vs. safety (t 28 = 0.60, p=0.55) in the last 1 s cue interval
outcomes.notes: Danger against uncertainty t = 1.94, p = 0.062, difference 0.24 Z (dz 0.36); uncertainty against safety t = 0.58, p = 0.57, difference 0.06 (paper p = 0.10 and 0.55). The type baseline gives p = 0.080 and 0.62.

outcomes.statement: Ramping population firing (100 ms bins over the cue) shows main effects of cue and bin and a cue x bin interaction, with ramping greatest to danger, intermediate to uncertainty and absent to safety.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 2; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: Ramping activity was most apparent to danger, intermediate to uncertainty, and absent to safety

statistics.about: main effects of cue and bin

outcomes.notes: Cue F(2,26) = 32.10, bin F(109,1417) = 12.29, cue x bin F(218,2834) = 4.29 (paper 4.33), all p < 1e-7. Last 1 s mean Z firing is danger 1.93, uncertainty 1.20 and safety -0.10.

outcomes.statement: Ramping neurons show no differential firing in the first 1 s cue interval.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 2; Figure 2D, left
outcomes.quote: Ramping neurons showed no significant differences in firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t 13 = 0.62, p=0.55) or uncertainty vs. safety (t 13 = 0.24, p=0.81) in the first 1 s cue interval
outcomes.notes: Danger against uncertainty t(13) = 0.43, p = 0.67 (difference 0.06); uncertainty against safety t = 0.49, p = 0.63 (0.04). The type baseline gives p = 0.54 and 0.77.

outcomes.statement: In the last 1 s cue interval Ramping neurons fire more to danger than to uncertainty and more to uncertainty than to safety.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 2; Figure 2D, right
outcomes.quote: However, differential firing to danger vs. uncertainty (t 13 = 3.17, p=7.41×10 −3 ), and uncertainty vs. safety (t 13 = 8.26, p=2.00×10 −6 ), was observed in the last 1 s cue interval
outcomes.notes: Danger above uncertainty t(13) = 3.14, p = 0.0078; uncertainty above safety t = 8.09, p = 2.0e-6 (paper 3.17 and 8.26). The type baseline gives the same.

outcomes.statement: Ramping population firing departs from safety earlier for danger (2.8 s after cue onset at p < 0.05, 5.8 s with Bonferroni correction) than for uncertainty (5.7 s, 6.5 s).
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 3; Methods, Population and single-unit firing analyses, paragraph 2; Figure 2E
outcomes.quote: Ramping activity to danger emerged earlier ( Figure 2E ; 2.8 s following cue onset for p<0.05; 5.8 s for full Bonferroni correction, p<0.00025 [0.05/200]) than ramping activity to uncertainty (5.7 s following cue onset; 6.5 s for full Bonferroni correction)
outcomes.notes: Danger departs from safety before uncertainty at both thresholds under every reading. With measure a and window starts (the first readings listed, given as measured), the times are 2.7, 4.5, 5.1 and 6.4 s against 2.8, 5.8, 5.7 and 6.5. Measure b gives 2.7, 4.7, 5.2 and 6.4 s, with three of four within tolerance. Window ends put every time 1 s later (3.7, 5.5, 6.1 and 7.4 s with measure a, 3.7, 5.7, 6.2 and 7.4 s with measure b). There the danger time at p < 0.00025 is within 5.8 +- 0.58, but the danger time at p < 0.05 (3.7 s against 2.8 +- 0.28) and the uncertainty time at p < 0.00025 (7.4 s against 6.5 +- 0.65) are not. No reading puts all four times within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: The rate of firing increase from the departure window to the last 1 s window does not differ between danger and uncertainty, so the earlier departure, not a faster rise, separates them.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 3; Figure 2E inset
outcomes.quote: Change in firing rate did not differ between danger and uncertainty ( Figure 2E , Inset)
outcomes.notes: No reading of fig2e-departure-times matched in full, so both measures are shown. Measure a gives danger 0.275 and uncertainty 0.288 Z/s, t(13) = -0.20, p = 0.84. Measure b gives t = -0.49, p = 0.63.

outcomes.statement: The population patterns hold trial by trial. Onset population firing in the first 1 s exceeds baseline on every individual trial of every cue, and Ramping population firing in the last 1 s exceeds baseline on danger and uncertainty trials but not safety trials.
outcomes.source: Figure 2, figure supplement 1
outcomes.quote: Note that increased cue firing over baseline tended to be highest on trial 1, but was observed for every individual trial for all cues ... Increased cue firing over baseline was consistently observed on danger and uncertainty trials, but not safety trials
outcomes.notes: Onset first-interval firing exceeds the population baseline at all 32 trial positions (smallest margin 5.3 spikes/s). Ramping last-interval firing exceeds it at all 22 danger and uncertainty positions and at 6 of the 10 safety positions, where the criterion's reading allows at most 5. Four of the six safety margins are below 3.4 spikes/s and two are 9.0 and 10.6. The notebook now prints the criterion's verdict (not met in full).
deviations: The paper gives no rule for "not safety trials"; the criterion's reading (at most half) is used.

outcomes.statement: Onset and Ramping firing is not driven by nose poke cessation. Across neurons, firing to danger (Onset first interval, Ramping last interval) is uncorrelated with firing to the first second of an ITI poke cessation and is consistently greater.
outcomes.source: Figure 2, figure supplement 2; Results, Population biases are evident in vlPAG single-units, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Comparison of single-unit firing to danger (Onset, first interval; Ramping, last interval) and nose poke suppression (first interval) revealed no correlation and an overwhelming bias towards greater firing to danger
outcomes.notes: With differential firing (measure b), Onset danger firing does not correlate with cessation firing (R2 = 0.0006, p = 0.90) and is greater in 26 of 29 neurons (sign p = 1.5e-5). Ramping gives R2 = 0.23, p = 0.080, and 14 of 14 (p = 1.2e-4; paper 1.22e-4). This holds under both ITI readings (median 166 to 241 events per neuron). With raw rates (measure a) the correlations are significant (R2 0.61 to 0.68), as a neuron's overall rate sets both values.
deviations: The -1 interval is read as the second ending at the poke and +1 as the second after it; the window from 1 s before to 2 s after the poke must lie in the ITI. The legend does not fix these.

outcomes.statement: In the four sessions with an Onset and a Ramping neuron recorded together, trial by trial firing of the two is not negatively related; a significant negative beta appears for one interval of one pair only.
outcomes.source: Results, vlPAG neurons show differential firing that is maximal to danger, paragraph 4; Figure 3
outcomes.quote: A significant (p<0.05), negative β was only found for one interval, for one neuron pair (pair 1, interval indicated by +)
outcomes.notes: Three Onset-Ramping pairs share a session, in two sessions (dr01101616, one pair; dr01102316, two Onset neurons with one Ramping neuron), against four pairs in four sessions in the paper. None of the 30 interval regressions gives a negative beta at p < 0.05 (betas -0.33 to 0.42), under both Z readings. The independence holds for the pairs found, and the pair count does not match. The criterion names neither case, so the outcome is partial. Nine units outside the populations have screen p from 0.025 to 0.046 and would each add a pair if they passed (five late-responsive LFR units in a session with an Onset neuron, four onset-responsive units in a session with a Ramping neuron), so the fourth pair may differ from these by a small change in the screen.

outcomes.statement: In the first 1 s interval, Onset single units' danger and uncertainty firing are correlated and biased to danger; uncertainty and safety firing are correlated but the bias to uncertainty is not significant; danger firing is biased to the first over the last interval, with no correlation between them.
outcomes.source: Results, Population biases are evident in vlPAG single-units, paragraph 1; Figure 4A to 4C; Methods, Population and single-unit firing analyses, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Danger and uncertainty firing were correlated, and single-units were biased towards greater firing to danger ( Figure 4A ). Uncertainty and safety firing were also correlated; however, the single-unit bias towards greater firing to uncertainty was not significant
outcomes.notes: A: r = -0.47, p = 0.010, danger greater in 22 of 29 (p = 0.008). B: r = -0.55, p = 0.002, uncertainty greater in 17 of 29 (p = 0.46). C: first greater in 22 of 29 (p = 0.008), r = 0.34, p = 0.070. The type baseline gives the same outcome. Both significant correlations are negative. Interval Z firing has mean zero over each neuron's 32 trials (6 D + 16 U + 10 S = 0), so a neuron's cue means trade off. With each neuron's trials shuffled (2000 times), A gives a median r of -0.49 (95% range -0.73 to -0.15) and B -0.68 (-0.84 to -0.43); the observed -0.47 and -0.55 lie within them. The criterion's correlations are present, but no stronger than the Z-scoring gives without a relation between cues. The text gives no sign.

outcomes.statement: The most common pattern of Onset neurons in the first 1 s interval is danger > uncertainty > safety (14 neurons), the only pattern with more neurons than expected by chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Population biases are evident in vlPAG single-units, paragraph 1; Figure 4D; Methods, Determining observed and expected cue firing patterns
outcomes.quote: Examining relative cue firing for each Onset neuron in the first 1 s interval revealed the most common pattern to be ... danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 14). This was the only pattern to contain more units than would be expected than chance
outcomes.notes: 14 of 29 Onset neurons are danger > uncertainty > safety, the largest of the four categories. With the three values permuted within each neuron (shuffle a), it is the only category above chance under both rules (95th percentile 8.05, whisker 9.0). With each cue permuted across neurons (shuffle b), its chance median is 15, and only safety > uncertainty > danger (4 against 3.5) is above chance. The criterion asks for one reading; the claim holds under shuffle a.

outcomes.statement: In the last 1 s interval, Ramping single units' danger and uncertainty firing are correlated and biased to danger; uncertainty and safety firing are not correlated but are biased to uncertainty; danger firing is biased to the last over the first interval, with no correlation between them.
outcomes.source: Results, Population biases are evident in vlPAG single-units, paragraph 2; Figure 4E to 4G
outcomes.quote: A significant correlation between firing to danger and uncertainty was observed, along with a single-unit bias towards greater firing to danger ( Figure 4E ). Only now, there was no correlation between uncertainty and safety firing, but a consistent bias towards greater uncertainty firing
outcomes.notes: E: danger greater in 12 of 14 (p = 0.013), but the correlation is not significant (r = -0.45, p = 0.11; type baseline p = 0.17). F: r = -0.46, p = 0.094, uncertainty greater in 14 of 14 (p = 1.2e-4). G: last greater in 12 of 14 (p = 0.013), r = 0.28, p = 0.33. Two of three panels hold. With trials shuffled within neuron, E gives a median r of -0.49 (95% range -0.80 to 0.01) and F -0.70 (-0.89 to -0.25); the observed -0.45 and -0.46 lie within them.

outcomes.statement: The most common pattern of Ramping neurons in the last 1 s interval is danger > uncertainty > safety (11 neurons), the only pattern above chance.
outcomes.source: Results, Population biases are evident in vlPAG single-units, paragraph 2; Figure 4H
outcomes.quote: The most common firing pattern in the last 1 s interval was ... danger > uncertainty > safety (n = 11). This was the only pattern to contain more units than expected by chance
outcomes.notes: 12 of 14 Ramping neurons are danger > uncertainty > safety, the largest category. It is the only category above chance under shuffle a (95th percentile 5, whisker 6). Under shuffle b no category is above chance (chance median 11).

outcomes.statement: In the first 1 s cue interval the Onset population's probability beta is positive and significant and exceeds both fear betas, neither of which differs from zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Onset neurons signal threat probability, paragraph 2; Figure 5A
outcomes.quote: The beta coefficient for the probability regressor was positive and significant, exceeding the beta coefficient for either measure of fear output – neither of which differed from zero
outcomes.notes: Under the primary reading (2 s interval fear, 20 s total fear, 0/0 set to 1, trial baseline, the reading the Methods regression table fixes), mean betas are probability 0.863, total fear 0.024 and interval fear -0.034. Probability exceeds total fear (t(28) = 3.74, p = 8.5e-4; paper 3.75) and interval fear (t = 4.55, p = 9.6e-5; paper 4.57). It is above zero (p = 6.2e-5), and the fear betas are not (p = 0.79, 0.58). All 18 readings of the amended claims file meet the criterion, also at 0.05. The answer to this attempt's question amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: the readings are now (interval fear window, total fear window) 2 s and 10 s, 2 s and 20 s, or 10 s and 20 s, with 0/0 set to 0, left out or set to 1, 18 readings with detail 4. The earlier run used 2 s and 20 s with 0/0 = 1 beside the claims file's same-window readings (2 s or 10 s for both ratios); those are shown as former readings and no longer count. All 12 former readings also met it; the outcome is unchanged.

outcomes.statement: Onset single-unit betas are positively biased for threat probability but not for total or interval fear.
outcomes.source: Results, Onset neurons signal threat probability, paragraph 2; Figure 5B and 5C
outcomes.quote: Single-unit beta coefficients were positively biased for threat probability, but not for either measure of fear output
outcomes.notes: Under the primary reading (2 s interval fear, 20 s total fear, 0/0 set to 1, trial baseline, the reading the Methods regression table fixes), probability betas are positive in 22 of 29 (sign p = 0.008). Interval fear (14 of 29, p = 1.0) and total fear (17 of 29, p = 0.46) are not biased. 17 of 18 readings of the amended claims file agree. With 2 s and 20 s windows, 0/0 trials left out and the trial baseline, probability is 20 of 29 (p = 0.061). The answer to this attempt's question amended details 1 and 2 of the claims file: the readings are now (interval fear window, total fear window) 2 s and 10 s, 2 s and 20 s, or 10 s and 20 s, with 0/0 set to 0, left out or set to 1, 18 readings with detail 4. The earlier run used 2 s and 20 s with 0/0 = 1 beside the claims file's same-window readings (2 s or 10 s for both ratios); those are shown as former readings and no longer count. The one reading that differs is the same as before; the outcome and the assumption are unchanged.
deviations: The readings differ in outcome. The outcome is under the primary reading, reading b of detail 1 and reading c of detail 2 with the trial baseline (reading a of detail 4), the reading that reproduces the Methods regression table on one unit (data check of the notebook).

findings.statement: The data description says the cube's poke.base is the nose poke rate 2 s before the cue. The data set's cubeScript.m computes it over the 20 s before onset, and uses it for every suppression ratio in the cube, including the 1 s and 500 ms intervals.
The paper and the description give a mean ITI of 3.5 min, but cue onsets are 132 to 195 s apart (mean about 2.7 min) in all 88 sessions, so no interval between cues reaches 3.5 min.

Five pairs of units recorded in the same session share 66 to 90% of the spikes of one unit within 0.5 ms (dr01092016 SPK10a and SPK14a; dr02092716 SPK04a and SPK15b; rf02091816 SPK01a and SPK04a; rf02110216 SPK08a and SPK13a; rf03110916 SPK04a and SPK14a). They may be one neuron sorted twice. The paper counts all 245 units, and one of these (dr02092716 SPK04a) is an Onset neuron.

The spike trains in the data set's files hold spikes only from 20 s before each cue onset to 31 to 34 s after it (34 of 12,261,110 spikes fall outside), with gaps of about 141 s between trials. The data description does not say so. A rate over the span of a unit's spike train is therefore about a third of its firing rate, and the files cannot give a whole-session rate.

paper_notes.statement: Neither the paper nor the data description states the nose poke baselines of the suppression ratios or how a 0/0 ratio is handled. The paper's printed regression input is reproduced by one unit only with a 2 s baseline for interval fear, a 20 s baseline for total fear and 0/0 set to 1. Other choices change the outcomes of fig1d-interval-suppression and fig1s1a-nose-poke-rates. Question for the authors: are these the windows and the rule used throughout, and which baseline does Figure 1, figure supplement 1A plot?

The data set's cubeScript.m computes the total and the interval suppression ratios over the 20 s baseline (poke.base, used in cer.cue and cer.s1.interval), while the paper's interval fear (its regression table, and the Figure 1D statistics) uses the 2 s baseline. The script also rounds the 2 s baseline firing rate down to an integer; the paper's table uses the unrounded rate, and the rounded one would change the Onset screen to 31 neurons.

The paper reports four Onset-Ramping pairs in four sessions. With the populations that match the paper's counts (29 and 14), only three pairs share a session, in two sessions. The paper's lists of Onset and Ramping units (Figure 1, figure supplements 4 and 6) are in figures only, and the data set does not mark which units the paper placed in each population.

Interval Z firing (Methods, Z-score normalization) has mean zero over each neuron's 32 trials, so its cue means satisfy 6 D + 16 U + 10 S = 0. Cross-neuron correlations of the cue means, as in Figure 4A, 4B, 4E and 4F, are then negative even with the trial labels shuffled (median r -0.49 to -0.70), and the observed correlations (-0.45 to -0.55) lie within the shuffled range.

The shuffle behind the chance levels of Figure 4D and 4H is not defined beyond "each neurons firing pattern was shuffled". Permuting within neurons reproduces the claims, and permuting each cue across neurons does not. Question for the authors: which shuffle was used?

The sliding-window departure times of Figure 2E depend on the firing measure and on whether a window is timed by its start or end, which the paper does not state. No reading gives all four times. By window start the Bonferroni danger time is 4.5 to 4.7 s against 5.8 s; by window end it is 5.5 to 5.7 s, but the danger time at p < 0.05 is then 3.7 s against 2.8 s. Question for the authors: which measure and time point were used?

entries.name: wright-2019
entries.title: Threat probability in ventrolateral periaqueductal gray neurons (Wright and McDannald 2019)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Wright and McDannald (2019) on CRCNS data set pag-1, which holds the spike times, event times and mean waveforms of 245 ventrolateral periaqueductal gray units recorded in 88 fear discrimination sessions of six rats. It recomputes suppression ratios, the k-means clusters, the Onset and Ramping populations, their population and single-unit firing, and the single-unit regressions on threat probability and fear output, under every reading of the details the paper leaves open and the reading the paper's printed regression input fixes.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Wright and McDannald (2019) from CRCNS pag-1
